passage:
"Papa, I got picked for the hackathon team too!" Aadhya dropped her bag by the door.
"Wah! That's my girl," Samir said, looking up from the newspaper. "The research internship, the college magazine, and now this?"
"And I said yes to the fest committee. They said nobody else could handle sponsorship."
"Of course they did." He smiled, then paused. "When did you last sleep before one?"
"Papa, sleep is for after placements." She laughed and opened the fridge. "Is there any of that leftover pulao?"
"You ate standing up yesterday also."
"Because I had a call at eight."
Samir folded the paper slowly. "Beta, I keep saying well done for everything you finish. I don't think I've once asked if you're enjoying any of it."
Aadhya closed the fridge. "Some of it."
"Which part? Tell me that part."

qa.q: Which committee did Aadhya say yes to?
qa.a: The fest committee, to handle sponsorship.

qa.q: What does Samir's slow folding of the newspaper suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He is growing uneasy and concerned, realising his praise may have been rewarding her overload.

qa.q: What shift in Samir's praise could help Aadhya?
qa.a: Asking what she enjoys and noticing her rest and limits, not only congratulating each new result.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when Samir asks which part she enjoys?
qa.a: She pauses, perhaps caught off guard and a little relieved to be asked about enjoyment instead of results.

grounding: Shows a parent praising a proud student's growing list of commitments, then noticing that praise for output alone rewards overload.

subtype: Stage 5: Body and mood sound the alarm [Actor]
passage: "Elizabeth, you asked why I've been so short with everyone. Okay. So. For about two months I've had a headache almost every afternoon, right behind the eyes. My stomach's been a mess; I eat and then it churns. Last week my brother asked me to pass the salt and I snapped at him like he'd insulted me. And Sunday nights, around seven, this dread comes. I feel it in my chest as the weekend ends. I kept thinking something was wrong with me, that I'm weak, that the other engineers on my team handle the release schedule just fine. Then my mother said something that stuck: 'Parul, your body is telling you about the schedule, not about you.' So I've booked a doctor for Thursday. And I'm going to show my manager the hours I've logged."

qa.q: When does the dread come each week?
qa.a: On Sunday nights, around seven, as the weekend ends.

qa.q: How did Parul feel about the symptoms at first?
qa.a: Parul felt ashamed and weak, assuming the problem was a personal flaw while teammates coped fine.

qa.q: Which steps is Parul taking, and why are they sensible?
qa.a: Parul has booked a doctor for Thursday and will show the manager the logged hours, treating the schedule, not weakness, as the problem.

qa.q: How might Parul's brother have experienced the snap over the salt?
qa.a: He probably felt stung and confused, since a simple request got a reply as if he had insulted Parul.

grounding: Shows a young engineer with headaches, stomach trouble, irritability at home and Sunday-night dread, signals that point to the schedule.

subtype: Stage 5: Body and mood sound the alarm [Observer]
passage:
Wednesday.
Abhinav snapped at the intern in standup today over a missing ticket. Abhinav, who used to bring laddoos on Fridays and remembered everyone's birthdays. He's forgotten two meetings this week, and his lunch box goes home full. Riya joked in the team group, "Someone needs a vacation!" and everyone sent laughing faces. He didn't reply.
I didn't want to add to that. At five I messaged him privately: "Coffee downstairs? No agenda." He came. I said he seemed really worn out and asked how he was actually doing. He was quiet, then said, "Headaches every day. I can't switch off." I didn't tell him to rest and it would pass. I said it might be worth seeing a doctor about the headaches and the sleep, and offered to cover his review slot on Friday if he wanted to go.
He said, "Thanks, Nandini. Nobody asked like that." I hope he goes.

qa.q: What did Riya write in the team group?
qa.a: "Someone needs a vacation!"

qa.q: Why did Nandini choose a private message instead of joining the group joke?
qa.a: Nandini felt concerned and protective, not wanting to add to Abhinav's embarrassment in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why is suggesting a doctor better than simply telling Abhinav to rest?
qa.a: Daily headaches and poor sleep may need proper care, and offering to cover the review slot makes going easier.

qa.q: What might the private coffee have felt like for Abhinav?
qa.a: He seemed relieved and cared for, saying nobody had asked like that before.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a once-cheerful teammate turn sharp, forgetful and skip lunch, and choosing a private check-in and a doctor over group jokes.

passage: "Jomon, sit. You've been here till ten every night this month, so I'm going to tell you something I don't tell many people. When I was twenty-five, in my first design job, I said yes to everything for a whole year. One Monday, the day of the biggest client deadline of my life, I woke up and could not get out of bed. I don't mean I didn't want to. My arms would not lift the blanket. I cried, I slept, I woke, I slept, through the whole day and into Tuesday. My roommate Mercy called my manager and then called a doctor. I felt like the worst failure in the world. Months later I understood it differently: my body took the rest I had refused it for a year. So this is your Usha ma'am telling you: go home at six today."

qa.q: What happened on the Monday of the big deadline?
qa.a: Usha woke up and could not get out of bed.

qa.q: How did young Usha feel about the crash at first?
qa.a: She felt like the worst failure in the world, ashamed that her body gave out on deadline day.

qa.q: What choice earlier in the story might have prevented young Usha's crash?
qa.a: Saying no to some of that year's requests, or telling the manager about the load before the deadline, might have prevented it.

qa.q: What might that Monday have been like for Mercy?
qa.a: Mercy was likely frightened to see Usha unable to get up, and acted by calling the manager and a doctor.

grounding: Shows a young designer crashing on a deadline Monday after a year of overwork, feeling it as failure, later seeing it as the body forcing rest.

passage: "Binita, beta, put the laptop down for five minutes; your Deepika Mausi wants to tell you something. When I was twenty-four, at the export house in Tiruppur, I was doing three people's jobs because I couldn't say no. I ate lunch at four and slept at two. One evening I sat down and wrote every task on one sheet of paper, with the hours each one took. The next morning I knocked on my manager's door, hands shaking, and said, 'This is my real load. I can do good work on half of it. Which half matters most?' I thought he would call me lazy. Instead he read it twice, moved two buyer accounts to Suresh and said, 'Why didn't you tell me in March?' After that I ate lunch at one. Tell your people early, beta. It costs so much less."

qa.q: What did Deepika write on the sheet of paper?
qa.a: Every task, with the hours each one took.

qa.q: How was young Deepika feeling as she knocked on the manager's door?
qa.a: She was nervous and afraid, her hands shaking, expecting to be called lazy.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things for Deepika?
qa.a: Writing down her real load and asking which half mattered most, instead of silently doing three people's jobs.

qa.q: How did the manager respond, and what does his question suggest?
qa.a: He read it twice and moved two accounts; asking why she did not tell him in March suggests he wished he had known sooner.

grounding: Shows a young worker telling her manager the truth about her load and handing off tasks, and the manager adjusting rather than blaming.

passage:
"Week six," Rajni said as they turned past the temple pond. "I did two half-days at the office. Just two."
"Just two," Parul repeated. "Three weeks ago you couldn't read an email."
"I know. Tuesday was good. I fixed a bug and actually laughed at lunch. Wednesday was flat. I stared at the screen and felt nothing."
"And?"
"And I didn't call it a failure. I went home, cooked with Amma and played carrom with my nephew. He beat me twice."
Parul grinned. "So Wednesday had carrom in it."
"It did." Rajni slowed down. "My counsellor asked me who I am when I'm not producing anything. I didn't have an answer in March."
"Do you now?"
"Someone who walks with you on Thursdays. Someone who loses at carrom. It's a start."

qa.q: How many half-days did Rajni work in week six?
qa.a: Just two half-days at the office.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel on the flat Wednesday, and how was it handled?
qa.a: Rajni felt empty and numb at the screen, but did not call it a failure and turned to cooking and carrom instead.

qa.q: Which part of Rajni's approach supports recovery best?
qa.a: Returning in small steps while restoring walks, family and play, instead of judging each day by output.

qa.q: What is it like for Parul to walk with Rajni now?
qa.a: Parul seems glad and relieved, noticing how far Rajni has come since not being able to read an email.

grounding: Shows slow recovery from burnout with good and flat days, a stepwise return to work, restored walks, family and play, and worth beyond output.

passage: At the Ram Navami bhajan in the village temple, a girl only a few years older than Anjali played the harmonium so fast her fingers blurred, and the whole courtyard clapped along. Walking home under the neem trees, Anjali could not stop talking. "Indu Bua, I'm going to play harmonium every single day. Every day! Even Sundays. Even when it rains." At home she pulled Dadi's old harmonium out from under the cot, blew off the dust and pumped the bellows until it wheezed. She pressed the same three keys for an hour, grinning, and drew a chart with thirty boxes on the back of a calendar page. Indu Bua smiled. "Let's see how the boxes look after the mela is over."

qa.q: How many boxes did Anjali draw on her chart?
qa.a: Thirty boxes, on the back of a calendar page.

qa.q: What feeling was driving Anjali's big promise?
qa.a: She was excited and inspired after watching the older girl play so fast, and wanted to play like her.

qa.q: What could help Anjali keep going once the excitement fades?
qa.a: A small, fixed practice time and someone to play for now and then, so it does not depend on excitement alone.

qa.q: Why might Indu Bua smile at the promise?
qa.a: Indu Bua enjoys Anjali's excitement but hints, with the remark about the mela, that the promise will be harder to keep later.

grounding: Shows a child announcing a daily practice plan right after watching someone admired, driven by excitement that makes starting easy.

passage: In Room 14 of the boys' hostel, a calendar hung beside Wasim's bunk with fourteen fat green ticks. Every morning since the first of the month he had been up at 5:45 for revision before the bell, and every night he ticked the day with a satisfied click of the pen. "Streak king," Hemant called him, and Wasim liked the name more than he admitted. He had started telling juniors, "I'm a morning person now." On day fifteen the warden announced a late-night inter-house quiz, and afterwards Wasim lay awake staring at the calendar. If he slept through the alarm, the fifteenth box would stay empty. The thought made his stomach turn, as if one blank square would cancel all fourteen ticks and prove he had never really changed.

qa.q: How many ticks were on Wasim's calendar?
qa.a: Fourteen fat green ticks.

qa.q: Why did the thought of an empty box make Wasim's stomach turn?
qa.a: He feels anxious because the streak has become who he is, so one miss feels like proof he never changed.

qa.q: What could Wasim tell himself about a possible missed morning?
qa.a: That one blank square after a late quiz is a normal slip, and restarting the next morning keeps the habit alive.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Wasim's streak?
qa.a: Hemant seems to admire it, teasing him fondly as the streak king, perhaps without seeing the pressure it adds.

grounding: Shows a teen proud of a two-week routine that has become part of who he is, so a single possible slip feels like a disaster.

passage: Week three, and the power had been out in the colony since the evening thunderstorm. Sarita sat on the steps with her English vocabulary cards and a candle stub. Eighteen days of ten new words a day, and her mock-test score had moved by exactly two marks. The cards felt like chewing paper. Just skip today, a voice in her head said reasonably. It's dark. One day won't matter. You'll do double tomorrow. Her younger brother Sumit was already lying on the cool floor, fanning himself with a notebook. "Didi, you're not doing cards in this, are you?" She almost said no. Instead she picked out five cards, not ten, and read them aloud to the candle. It was boring. She did it anyway, then blew out the flame.

qa.q: How much had Sarita's mock-test score moved?
qa.a: By exactly two marks.

qa.q: What does the voice telling Sarita to skip suggest about her mood?
qa.a: She is bored and discouraged, so her mind bargains that one skipped day in the dark will not matter.

qa.q: Why was doing five cards instead of ten a wise choice?
qa.a: A smaller version kept the habit going on a hard, boring day, relying on discipline rather than mood.

qa.q: What would change if Sarita had taken Sumit's hint and skipped?
qa.a: The first skip could make the next one easier, and the routine might quietly fade.

grounding: Shows a routine turning dull in week three with slow results, the mind bargaining to skip once, and discipline carrying the effort instead of mood.

passage:
Gopika,
You asked about my sketching challenge. Honest answer: it's dead. I was at 41 days straight, one drawing every night, posting them in our little group. Then Chachu's wedding in Lucknow happened. Four days of haldi, sangeet and relatives in every room. No table, no quiet. I told myself I'd catch up on the train back. I didn't.
When I got home and saw the empty days in my sketchbook, I felt so guilty I shut it. The streak was already broken, so what was the point of drawing that night, or the next? That was nearly three weeks ago. The sketchbook is still under a pile of wedding sweet boxes.
The stupid thing is, I miss it. I just can't face starting again from day one.
Alka

qa.q: How many days in a row had Alka sketched before the wedding?
qa.a: 41 days straight, one drawing every night.

qa.q: Why did Alka shut the sketchbook after coming home?
qa.a: Alka felt guilty and defeated seeing the empty days, and decided the streak was ruined anyway.

qa.q: What could Alka try instead of starting again from day one?
qa.a: Alka could do one small sketch tonight and count it as picking up, not restarting, so one trip does not end the habit.

qa.q: How might Gopika read this email?
qa.a: Gopika may feel sympathetic and see what Alka cannot yet: four days away did not undo 41 days of drawing.

grounding: Shows a routine broken by a trip, guilt about the gap, and all-or-nothing thinking that turns a few missed days into stopping altogether.
